q: When does the advanced phase of TFP begin?
o: When idealized and persecutory segments can be held in emotional continuity
After exactly 2 years of twice-weekly sessions, whatever the progress
When all symptoms have disappeared and acting out has stopped
When medication has been successfully tapered and stopped
e: The advanced phase begins when split-off persecutory and idealized developments have been sufficiently worked through that the patient can tolerate both segments in emotional continuity, without reenacting them in a split-off way (with temporary loss of reality testing and massive projection). The patient now understands emotionally that he identifies with both the self and the object of each dyad. In the book's example, the integration of love and hate under the dominance of love, fleetingly and then more consistently, marked the beginning of the advanced stage. It is defined by structure, not by the calendar or symptom checklists.
w: TFP does not set a fixed calendar point; the timing varies from 6 months to years.
Symptoms and acting out often improve earlier; the marker is integration of split segments, not a symptom-free state.
Medication changes are not a criterion; the criterion is psychological integration in the transference.
k: Advanced phase = the patient can hold idealized and persecutory segments in emotional continuity without split-off reenactment.
h: Two halves of the movie now play on one screen, in sequence, without the projector breaking.

q: How soon can the advanced phase emerge, and which patients reach it faster?
o: From 6 months to years; less antisocial, paranoid or narcissistic patients get there faster
Always after about 5 years of treatment; personality features have no effect on the timing
Always at about 1 year, once the early phase is complete
Only narcissistic patients reach it, and only after several years
e: The advanced phase can come as early as 6 months into treatment or take years. Patients who are less antisocial, paranoid or narcissistic generally get there more quickly, because those features are the main obstacles: antisocial features block honest communication, paranoid features keep the bad object projected, and narcissistic features defend against dependency on the therapist. Clinically, this means a therapist treating a malignant narcissistic patient should expect a long road, while an infantile or histrionic patient without these features may integrate faster.
w: No fixed duration applies, and personality features strongly affect the pace.
There is no standard one-year point; the early phase has no fixed length either.
Narcissistic features slow progress; they don't define the only patients who reach the advanced phase.
k: Advanced phase: from 6 months to years; antisocial, paranoid and narcissistic features slow it down.
h: The 'APN' brakes: Antisocial, Paranoid, Narcissistic.

q: How do regressions in the advanced phase differ from earlier ones?
o: They are worked through in a few sessions, eventually within one
They disappear entirely once the advanced phase begins
They last longer than before, for weeks at a time
They usually require brief hospitalization
e: Regressions still occur in the advanced phase, sometimes looking like an exact repeat of the first sessions, with splitting, projection and omnipotent control. The difference is speed: they no longer last days or weeks but are worked through in several sessions and eventually within one. The three interpretive steps, (1) recognizing the dominant object relation, (2) defining self and object representations and their interchange, and (3) integrating the split-off dyads, become condensed into a single or a few sessions, with a gradual decrease in regressive tendencies.
w: Regressions still occur; integration alternates with brief regression even in the advanced phase.
Lasting weeks describes earlier phases; now they resolve faster.
Hospitalization is not the typical response; the regression is worked through in sessions.
k: Advanced-phase regressions still happen but are worked through in a few sessions, eventually within one.
h: Same storm, shorter forecast.

q: Why are depressive transferences more advanced than paranoid ones?
o: They rest on beginning integration of good and bad images, with mourning of the ideal
They involve more intense anxiety and more frequent acting out than paranoid ones
They involve psychotic distortions of the therapist that test reality more severely
They are based on more radical splitting between all-good and all-bad images
e: Psychopathic and paranoid transferences rest on primitive, split-off representations, such as the evil other menacing a helpless self, coexisting with a submerged dyad of a perfect provider caring for a beloved self. Depressive transferences rest on the beginning integration of good and bad images into a more realistic view of others. That integration brings depressive affect: the loss and mourning of the ideal object that splitting had protected. They begin to resemble the transferences of neurotic patients and signal the resolution of identity diffusion.
w: Depressive transferences are less chaotic, with less acting out; intensity of anxiety isn't what makes them advanced.
Psychotic distortion is not a feature of depressive transferences.
Radical splitting describes the paranoid and psychopathic transferences, not the depressive ones.
k: Depressive transferences rest on integration of good and bad images, with mourning of the ideal object.
h: To see the whole person, you must bury the perfect one.

q: Can one speak of an advanced stage before psychopathic transferences are fully resolved?
o: No – honest communication must be reliable first
Yes, as long as symptoms and acting out have improved
Yes, always, regardless of honesty
Only for narcissistic patients
e: The book is explicit: one cannot really speak of an advanced stage before psychopathic transferences are fully resolved. Honest communication does not rule out occasional secrets or temporary suppression out of shame or paranoid fear, but in general the therapist must be able to rely on the patient's honesty to resolve such breakdowns. Psychopathic transferences resolve when the patient can doubt the assumption that the therapist is totally exploitative, incapable of empathy, and that the relationship is only about who can use whom.
w: Symptom improvement isn't enough; without honest communication there is no reliable material to work with.
Honesty is a precondition; dishonesty blocks any advanced work.
This applies to all patients, not just narcissistic ones.
k: No advanced phase without resolving psychopathic transferences: honest communication must be generally reliable.
h: You can't build the upper floors on a foundation of lies.
r: Clarkin Ch9 – Resolution of psychopathic transferences

q: In the advanced phase, paranoid transferences:
o: They may appear but resolve within a session or days
They never occur once the advanced phase begins
They last for months, as in the early phase
They mean the treatment has failed
e: Unlike psychopathic transferences, paranoid transferences may still be strongly present in the advanced phase. What changes is that they resolve within a session or in days rather than weeks, and the therapeutic alliance (the bond between the therapist in role and the patient's observing ego) is strong enough to tolerate them without threatening treatment. Within these no-longer-festering paranoid episodes, moments of guilt over aggression, acknowledged ambivalence and reparative strivings signal continuing integration.
w: Paranoid transferences can still appear; it's psychopathic ones that must be resolved.
Lasting months describes the early phase, not the advanced one.
A transient paranoid regression is expected, not a sign of failure.
k: Advanced-phase paranoid transferences can still appear but resolve within a session or days, held by a strong alliance.
h: Paranoia visits but no longer moves in.

q: Why might a therapist miss a patient's improvement outside sessions?
o: Turmoil in sessions can be dissociated from improvement outside
Patients deliberately hide improvement to stay in treatment
Improvement never happens outside sessions in BPO
Therapists in TFP never ask about outside life
e: As treatment progresses, severe acting out outside sessions should already be under control, while intense regression shows up as affect storms inside the sessions. Because of this turmoil, especially when the transference is intensely negative, the therapist can miss significant improvement outside: it is so dissociated from the sessions that he neglects to acknowledge changes in the patient's relationships. The lesson is to keep inquiring about outside life and to notice progress, not just the storm in the room.
w: Patients don't deliberately hide improvement; the dissociation between inside and outside causes it to be missed.
Improvement outside sessions often happens early in successful TFP.
TFP does inquire about outside life; the risk is that turmoil in the room distracts from it.
k: Session turmoil, especially in negative transference, can hide real improvement outside; keep asking about outside life.
h: Thunder in the room can drown out sunshine outside.

q: In the advanced phase, how does somatization typically change?
o: Patients look for the emotions behind complaints; it joins transference work
Somatization increases as aggression is no longer acted out in behavior
Somatic complaints are treated with medication only
Somatic complaints are ignored to avoid secondary gain
e: Patients who used to turn intrapsychic conflict into bodily complaints become able to experience emotional difficulties within themselves, with others and in the transference. When somatic complaints appear, they look for the emotional issue being avoided, and somatization becomes a natural part of transference exploration. In the book's example, a patient with infantile personality, bulimia and obesity linked her binges to transference developments, brought the temptation to binge into the sessions, and reduced bingeing more easily.
w: Somatization decreases, along with acting out, as conflict is experienced psychologically.
Medication alone is not the approach; somatic complaints become material for exploration.
Somatic complaints are explored for the emotions behind them, not ignored, in the advanced phase.
k: In the advanced phase, somatization becomes material: patients search for the emotion behind the complaint.
h: The body stops speaking for the mind.

q: Which is a sign of the advanced phase in the patient–therapist relationship?
o: The patient anticipates his comments and corrects distortions herself ('…though I know that's not true')
The patient stops talking, because nothing new remains to be said and the work is essentially done
The patient demands direct advice about decisions in work and love
The patient idealizes the therapist completely and accepts every comment
e: In the advanced phase, the patient may anticipate the therapist's comments, signalling internalization of the therapist's attitudes and a more realistic view of his personality. This realistic view strengthens the observing ego during regressions: 'What you're saying makes me think you're disgusted with me... though I know that's not true.' The patient holds the distorted perception and the reality at once. The relationship deepens, and the patient appreciates the therapist's contribution more realistically.
w: Patients talk more freely in the advanced phase; silence would suggest resistance, not completion.
Demanding direct advice is not a sign of advanced work; TFP stays exploratory.
Complete idealization is splitting; the advanced phase brings a realistic, mixed view.
k: Advanced-phase sign: the patient anticipates the therapist and corrects her own distortion ('though I know that's not true').
h: The patient carries a pocket therapist.

q: How does the interpretive approach change in the advanced phase?
o: More genetic interpretations, fuller dream analysis, more direct statements
Only here-and-now interpretations, avoiding any reference to the past
No interpretations, letting the patient work on her own
Only supportive comments to consolidate the gains made
e: In the advanced phase, the therapist can link present transference to unconscious past pathogenic object relations: genetic (psychogenic) interpretations join the here-and-now interpretations that dominated the early and middle phases. Free association and full classic dream analysis become possible (associating to each element of the manifest content), compared with the partial dream analysis used earlier. The therapist can be more direct and less tentative, relying more on the patient's observing ego.
w: Here-and-now work continues, but genetic links to the past are now added.
The therapist keeps interpreting; the patient's autonomous work increases but doesn't replace interpretation.
Supportive comments are not the TFP approach in any phase.
k: Advanced phase: more genetic interpretations, full dream analysis, and more direct statements.
h: Now the past can be invited into the room.

q: Regarding 'exploration of therapist comments', what is the key criterion?
o: Whether the patient reflects on it, versus automatic rejection or lip-service
Whether the patient explicitly agrees with each comment and adopts it
Whether the transference is currently positive or negative
How quickly the patient replies to the comment
e: The indicator is not whether the patient agrees with an interpretation, nor whether the transference is positive or negative. It is whether the patient gives himself the chance to reflect on what the therapist said, versus immediate automatic rejection, or thoughtless acceptance, submission and lip service. Expansion or further exploration of comments contrasts with earlier systematic disagreement without reflection. This is especially important with severe narcissistic patients and those using primitive defenses against acknowledging aggression.
w: Agreement can be lip service or submission, which the book counts as non-reflection.
The positive or negative tone of the transference is explicitly not the criterion.
The speed of reply is irrelevant; reflection is what matters.
k: Structural-change marker: reflecting on the therapist's comments, versus automatic rejection or lip-service agreement.
h: Not 'yes' or 'no', but 'let me think about that'.
r: Clarkin Ch9 – Indicators of structural change

q: Which triad is resolved in a type of aggressively narcissistic patient?
o: Arrogance, curiosity and pseudostupidity
Guilt, shame and envy
Splitting, denial and idealization
Anxiety, depression and anger
e: Among the indicators of containment of hatred, the book lists the resolution of the triad of arrogance, curiosity and pseudostupidity found in a type of aggressively narcissistic patient (a concept from Bion). The patient arrogantly dismisses, shows intrusive curiosity about the therapist, and acts as if unable to understand. Alongside its resolution come decreases in direct violence in sessions, aggressive dismissal of the therapist's comments, sadomasochistic transferences, envy-based negative therapeutic reactions, and self-directed hatred such as self-injury and substance abuse.
w: Guilt, shame and envy are affects, not the triad named.
Splitting, denial and idealization are primitive defenses.
Anxiety, depression and anger are general symptoms.
k: The arrogance–curiosity–pseudostupidity triad of aggressive narcissism resolves as hatred becomes contained.
h: The 'know-it-all who pries and plays dumb'.

q: Order the three negative therapeutic reactions (Table 9–2) from least to most severe:
o: Unconscious guilt → envy of the therapist → destructiveness as triumph
Envy of the therapist → unconscious guilt → destructiveness as triumph
Destructiveness as triumph → envy of the therapist → unconscious guilt
Unconscious guilt → destructiveness as triumph → envy of the therapist
e: Table 9–2 orders negative therapeutic reactions from least to most severe. First, unconscious guilt about improving, which can take the form of a masochistic transference. Second, envy of the therapist, typical of narcissistic patients: any improvement proves the therapist's superiority, so it is rejected. Third, the experience of destructiveness and self-destructiveness as triumph and power over others, over pain and illness, even over life and death, found in malignant narcissism and antisocial personality disorder.
w: This swaps the first two; guilt is the least severe and envy comes second.
This reverses the whole order; triumph through destruction is the most severe.
This swaps the last two; envy of the therapist precedes triumph through destructiveness.
k: Negative therapeutic reactions, mild to severe: guilt (masochistic) → envy (narcissistic) → destructiveness as triumph (malignant narcissism/ASPD).
h: G-E-T worse: Guilt, Envy, Triumph.

q: What complication can arise in advanced phases for patients with severe primary sexual inhibition?
o: Inhibition may grow as repression replaces splitting, sometimes needing sex therapy
Inhibition always resolves on its own once splitting is worked through
These patients usually become promiscuous as aggression is released
There is no complication; sexuality is unaffected by structural change
e: An active, even self-destructive sexual life is prognostically more favourable than severe primary inhibition of all sensual engagement. A specific complication in such inhibited patients is that, as functioning improves and repression replaces splitting and dissociation, the sexual inhibition may increase. This may require modifying the approach, such as combining with sex therapy once the unconscious dynamics of the inhibition have been clarified enough to integrate both treatments.
w: The book warns it can worsen; it doesn't resolve on its own.
The complication is more inhibition, not promiscuity.
Structural change does affect sexuality, sometimes increasing inhibition.
k: In primary sexual inhibition, improvement can increase inhibition as repression replaces splitting; sex therapy may be added.
h: Better defenses can shut the bedroom door tighter.

q: 'Does that sound like somebody we know?' – a patient's response to the therapist describing a friendly vs sadistic person. This illustrates:
o: Taking back projections (the stepmother representation inside her)
Psychotic confusion between her own identity and her stepmother's
An erotic transference toward the therapist
Denial of any similarity to the stepmother
e: The therapist described a person who is sometimes friendly and at other times hostile, sadistic, provoking and blind to it, asking whether he was two different persons or whether she saw something she struggled with inside. The patient's ironic 'Does that sound like somebody we know?' showed her beginning to take back the projection. The therapist said the image referred to both her and her stepmother, and to her colluding with the stepmother inside her. This follows Steiner: early on, examine the projected image without accepting or rejecting it; later the patient acknowledges it as intrapsychic.
w: She knew who was who; she was recognizing a shared internal image, not losing her identity.
The exchange concerned a sadistic image, not erotic feelings.
She was acknowledging the similarity, not denying it.
k: Taking back projections (recognizing the projected image as one's own) is a marker of structural change.
h: Steiner's sequence: first hold the mirror, later she sees herself in it.
r: Clarkin Ch9 – Capacity to use interpretation

q: Which is considered the most fundamental marker of entering the advanced stage?
o: A shift in predominant transference paradigms
A reduction in session frequency
The stopping of all medication
The patient's agreement with interpretations
e: A shift in predominant transference paradigms is the most fundamental marker of entering the advanced stages. Each patient has a limited number of transference patterns that repeat over months or years, each worked through in three interpretive steps: defining the relationship, identifying self and object and their interchange, and integrating split-off idealized and persecutory parts. In the advanced stage, new, more complex aspects of self and objects appear, transcending the rigid early patterns.
w: Session frequency does not change; TFP keeps the same intensity.
Stopping medication isn't a marker; the fundamental sign is a shift in predominant transference paradigms.
Agreement can be lip service; the shift in transference paradigm is what matters.
k: The most fundamental advanced-phase marker: a shift in predominant transference paradigms.
h: The play gets new characters.
r: Clarkin Ch9 – Shift in transference paradigms

q: A patient oscillating between a weak asexual father and a sadistic stepmother came to see the therapist as friendly, strong and sexually seductive. This reflects:
o: A new constellation from integration, with oedipal material
A regression to earlier pre-oedipal splitting
A psychotic distortion of the therapist's sexuality
Erotized acting out that threatens the frame
e: This patient had oscillated between seeing the therapist as a warm but weak, asexual father and a powerful, sadistic stepmother. After integrating these split images, she began to see him as friendly yet strong and sexually seductive: a totally new constellation. New aspects of her relationship with her father emerged with a markedly oedipal quality, in contrast to the pre-oedipal denial of all sexuality in the image of the idealized but weak father. Combining warmth with strength is integration, and the arrival of sexuality marks higher-level (oedipal) material.
w: Pre-oedipal splitting was the earlier pattern; this is the integration that followed it.
Seeing the therapist as sexually attractive here is not psychotic.
There was no acting out; this was a shift in transference experience.
k: Integration can produce a new transference constellation with oedipal material, replacing pre-oedipal split images.
h: Weak-and-kind plus strong-and-cruel became strong-and-kind, and the oedipal door opened.

q: An antisocial patient began feeling guilty about lying, saw the therapist as strict but concerned, and tried to repair friendships. This is:
o: A shift into a depressive transference
A psychopathic transference with manipulation
A paranoid regression
A narcissistic defense
e: This patient had long perceived the therapist as a persecutory, sadistic moralizer, protecting herself with secrets and manipulation. She began to feel guilty about her dishonesty and about mistreating the therapist, saw him as a strict but concerned father (unlike her manipulative, dishonest father), became depressed, felt she didn't deserve his care, and developed a quiet remorse, trying to repair friendships she had damaged. This is a clear shift into a depressive transference: guilt, feeling undeserving, remorse and reparation.
w: She stopped manipulating and felt guilty; that is the opposite of a psychopathic transference.
She didn't fear the therapist; she valued him, so this isn't paranoid.
She wasn't dismissing the therapist; she felt she didn't deserve him.
k: Guilt, feeling undeserving, quiet remorse and reparation = shift into a depressive transference.
h: From 'outwit the judge' to 'I'm sorry, let me fix it'.

q: What may happen with some narcissistic/malignant-narcissistic patients who improve?
o: The grandiose self consolidates at a more adaptive level and resists change
They always integrate fully once the grandiose self is interpreted
They become openly antisocial as narcissistic defenses weaken
They decompensate into psychosis when grandiosity is challenged
e: The most dramatic transference shift is the breakup of the pathological grandiose self, but it does not always happen. Some narcissistic and malignant narcissistic patients improve, gaining ego strength, while consolidating the grandiose self at a higher, more adaptive level and using it to defend against further change. Symptoms improve and turmoil decreases, but subtle, stubborn resistance remains. The therapist may move toward termination, recommending further treatment later (possibly standard psychoanalysis) if difficulties with intimacy persist.
w: Full integration does not always occur; some consolidate the grandiose self instead.
Becoming openly antisocial is not the pattern described.
Psychosis isn't the expected outcome; the grandiose self consolidates at a more adaptive level instead.
k: Some narcissistic patients improve while consolidating a more adaptive grandiose self that resists further change.
h: The fortress gets a nicer facade but keeps its walls.

q: A patient who succeeded in career and marriage refuses to explore persisting sexual inhibition. The book links this to:
o: Unconscious guilt over triumph over her siblings
Unconscious envy of the therapist's success
Psychopathic dishonesty about her sexual life
Side effects of medication on her libido
e: After years of hospitalization and confinement at home, this patient resumed studies, built a career, married and had children, but kept severe sexual inhibition she had no wish to explore. The book links this to unconscious guilt over triumph over her siblings, since she was doing much better than them. This is a guilt-based negative therapeutic reaction that comes with depressive transferences ('I'm not worthy of this'), which must be distinguished from envy-based reactions typical of narcissistic pathology.
w: Envy of the therapist is the narcissistic type of negative reaction, not the one described here.
There's no indication of dishonesty; she simply declined to explore.
Medication is not mentioned as a cause.
k: Refusing further improvement can be guilt-based (triumph over siblings), unlike envy-based narcissistic reactions.
h: 'I've won enough; more would hurt them.'
r: Clarkin Ch9 – Depressive transference and guilt

q: Masochistic transferences in the advanced phase may appear as:
o: Boredom, lost motivation, or emptying sessions so the therapist loses interest
Violent outbursts toward the therapist whenever progress is noticed or praised
Brief psychotic episodes triggered by success at work
A return to drug use to sabotage outside achievements
e: As normal superego functions develop, unconscious guilt (over pre-oedipal aggression toward the mother and oedipal guilt over success) can show up as masochistic transferences aimed at preventing further improvement. Clinically, they appear as boredom, loss of motivation for learning, or an unconscious effort to empty out the sessions so that the therapist loses interest. After a long, successful treatment, this can be mistaken for maximum benefit, missing that the patient feels unworthy of the gratification the relationship is beginning to provide.
w: Violent outbursts are not the described masochistic form; it's quieter, emptying out.
Psychotic episodes aren't described; masochistic transferences show quietly as boredom and emptied sessions.
A return to drug use is not the described pattern.
k: Advanced-phase masochistic transference: boredom, lost motivation, emptied sessions, which can be mistaken for maximum benefit.
h: A quiet sabotage that looks like a natural ending.

q: In antisocial patients, intensification of paranoid transferences in later treatment is generally:
o: Positive overall (psychopathic transferences transformed), but may need the incompatible-realities method
Always a sign of failure, showing that the antisocial structure cannot be changed by psychotherapy
Irrelevant, since paranoid feelings in antisocial patients carry no meaning
A sign that termination should begin before the regression worsens
e: In patients with significant antisocial features, worked-through psychopathic transferences may transform into paranoid tendencies. This is generally positive: previously distant, empty contact is replaced by intense paranoid enactments, meaning the relationship now matters. But paranoia can regress to delusional conviction in the transference, requiring the method of incompatible realities (Chapter 4, Tactic 3): the therapist states his opposite conviction and analyses the relationship between a 'normal' and a 'totally irrational' person in the room, leaving reality in suspension.
w: It is generally positive, not a sign of failure.
Paranoid feelings in this context carry meaning and must be explored.
It's a phase to work through, not a reason to end.
k: In antisocial patients, psychopathic → paranoid transference is progress; if it becomes delusional, use incompatible realities.
h: Fear is closer than indifference.
r: Clarkin Ch9 – Intensification of paranoid transferences

q: What attitude combination is advised in the advanced phase?
o: Impatience within each session, great patience for long-term working through
Patience within each session, combined with impatience about the overall rate of progress
Complete relaxation, since the hardest work is already done
Strict control of session content to prevent regression
e: The book advises impatience (versus complacency) within each session, combined with great patience for the long-term working through of dominant problems. Impatience in each session maintains momentum against the patient's subtle learning of how to keep a comfortable equilibrium, and guards against the therapist's natural tendency to relax because things seem to be going well. The therapist must resist being lulled into accepting the patient as he is, with a subtle restriction of treatment goals.
w: This reverses it: impatience belongs within each session and patience to the long term.
Relaxation is the danger the book warns against.
Strict control of content is not TFP technique; the therapist follows the material.
k: Advanced phase: impatience within each session, great patience for long-term working through.
h: Sprint each hour, marathon each year.

q: An art-therapy career initially imitating 'phony' professionals failed, then later succeeded authentically. What changed?
o: Resolution of a psychopathic transference that expected exploitation
Better professional training and supervision in art therapy
A change of medication that improved her judgment
A move to a different employer with clearer rules
e: The patient's interest in art therapy was partly an identification with qualities she saw in the therapist, but it began before idealized and persecutory images were integrated. Unconsciously she imitated what she saw as mental health professionals' 'phony' interest in patients (a projected persecutory image); lacking true commitment, she lost jobs through inappropriate interactions, including sharing drugs with patients. Once this psychopathic transference, expecting exploitation, was explored and resolved, her interest became an authentic commitment, and she became a highly respected therapist.
w: Training was not the difference; the change came from resolving the transference.
Medication isn't mentioned; the change came from resolving her psychopathic transference expecting exploitation.
The change came from within her, not from a new employer.
k: Resolving a psychopathic transference (expecting exploitation) can turn imitation into authentic commitment.
h: From faking care to really caring.

q: If oedipal transferences and primitive regressions coexist in the advanced phase, which takes priority?
o: Regressions to primitive transferences
Oedipal material, since it is more advanced
Whichever the patient prefers
Neither
e: In the advanced phase, more elaborate neurotic transferences may emerge, such as oedipal fears and fantasies or rivalry with other patients. But regressions to primitive transferences usually take priority, and the oedipal material may have to be set aside temporarily. The general principle (psychopathic before paranoid, paranoid before depressive) holds particularly true at this stage: interpret the most primitive, most disruptive material first.
w: Oedipal material is more advanced, but primitive regressions still take priority.
Priority follows the clinical principle, not the patient's preference.
Both are addressed, with primitive regressions first.
k: Primitive regressions take priority over oedipal material; psychopathic → paranoid → depressive order still holds.
h: Put out the fire before rearranging the furniture.

q: How do separation reactions change with integration?
o: From panic, rage or narcissistic denial to sadness, mourning and loneliness
From sadness and mourning to panic and fear of abandonment
They disappear completely, since the patient no longer needs the therapist
They become briefly psychotic before finally resolving
e: Earlier in treatment, separations (weekends, vacations, illness) provoke severe separation anxiety, panic and regressive behaviour, or, in narcissistic pathology, complete denial of dependency and a tendency to leave the therapist first. With integration, reactions become depressively tinged: mourning, sadness and loneliness rather than panic over being abandoned and mistreated. Analysing these reactions further integrates split-off transferences and prepares the patient for termination.
w: This reverses the direction; integration moves from panic toward sadness.
Separation reactions don't disappear; they become more mature.
Brief psychosis is not the expected path.
k: With integration, separation reactions move from panic, rage or denial to sadness, mourning and loneliness.
h: From 'you abandoned me!' to 'I'll miss you'.

q: According to Freud, normal mourning includes:
o: Sadness without guilt, introjection, gratification at being alive; ends in 6–12 months
Intense guilt and self-attack, with the lost object attacked inside the self, lasting for several years
No sadness at all, only relief and new relationships
Manic triumph over the lost object, without introjection
e: In 'Mourning and Melancholia', Freud described normal mourning as sadness and normal depression without guilt; introjection of the lost object (rebuilding it inside, becoming a bit like it); and a narcissistic gratification at being alive. Together these allow the mourning to be worked through, ending in 6 months to a year. Pathological mourning is severe, longer and guilt-laden: unconscious hostility once aimed at the object is turned against the self, now identified with the lost object.
w: Intense guilt and self-attack describe Freud's pathological mourning.
Normal mourning includes sadness; what it lacks, for Freud, is guilt.
Manic triumph is Klein's secondary defense, not Freud's normal mourning.
k: Freud's normal mourning: sadness without guilt, introjection, gratification at being alive; ends in 6–12 months.
h: Sad, rebuild them inside, glad to be alive.
r: Clarkin Ch9 – Normal and pathological separation

q: How does Klein's view of guilt in mourning differ from Freud's?
o: Klein: guilt is in normal and pathological mourning; intensity and sadism mark pathology
Klein: there is no guilt in either normal or pathological mourning, only persecutory anxiety
Freud: guilt is always present and normal, even in healthy mourning
They agree completely on the role of guilt and ambivalence in mourning
e: For Freud, guilt marks pathological mourning. For Klein, guilt is present all along, in both normal and pathological mourning: what defines pathology is the intensity of guilt and the sadism of the superego. Likewise, ambivalence is always there; pathology is the intolerance of it. In pathological mourning, aggression destroys the good internal object as well as the external one, leaving emptiness, with a vicious circle of guilt and possible regression to the paranoid-schizoid position or hypomanic defenses.
w: Klein sees guilt as present in both normal and pathological mourning.
Freud ties guilt to pathological mourning, not normal mourning.
They differ: Klein places guilt in normal mourning too.
k: Klein: guilt and ambivalence are in all mourning; pathology lies in intensity, sadism and intolerance of ambivalence.
h: Freud: guilt = sick. Klein: guilt = normal, cruelty = sick.

q: In Klein's depressive position, guilt leads to:
o: Reparation and gratitude
Splitting and projection
Projective identification
Psychotic regression
e: In the depressive position, the infant recognizes that his aggression was aimed at an object that is not all bad but mixed. Guilt develops as a normal affect, aimed at the self. It leads to wishes to repair the relationship with mother and do good things: reparation, which Klein saw as the origin of sublimatory tendencies. Gratitude becomes prevalent, with a longing for a good relationship with the external object.
w: Splitting and projection belong to the paranoid-schizoid position.
Projective identification is a primitive defense of the paranoid-schizoid position.
Guilt in the depressive position leads to repair, not psychosis.
k: Klein's depressive-position guilt leads to reparation (origin of sublimation) and gratitude.
h: Re-PAIR: guilt wants to put the pair back together.

q: In Klein's model, 'manic triumph' is:
o: A secondary defense against guilt: replacing the lost object with many relationships
A clinical manic episode triggered by the loss, requiring mood stabilizers and close monitoring
The normal end point of mourning, when the lost object is forgotten
A depressive symptom expressing guilt toward the lost object
e: Manic triumph is meant in a psychodynamic, not clinical, sense. In normal mourning, especially after a real death, guilt may be excessively reinforced; as a secondary defense there may be an unconscious wish to affirm one's freedom from the lost object and replace it with many other relationships, escaping the pain of guilt and loss. In pathological mourning, hypomanic defenses become exaggerated: triumph, contempt, identification with an idealized lost object, omnipotence, denial of mourning, and compulsive engagement in multiple relations without true engagement.
w: The book stresses it's psychodynamic, not a clinical manic episode.
Mourning ends with the object internalized, not forgotten.
It's a defense against guilt, not a depressive symptom.
k: Manic triumph: a secondary defense against guilt, affirming freedom from the lost object through many new relationships.
h: 'I don't need you, look how many friends I have!'

q: What is typical of the termination reaction in NEUROTIC organization?
o: Intense sadness, idealization, feeling unworthy, clinging – mild pathological mourning
Panic, rage and fear of abandonment, with destruction of the therapist's good internal image
No reaction, with immediate devaluation of the therapist and treatment
Moderate sadness with freedom, appreciation and readiness to go on
e: The book distinguishes termination by organization. Normal: moderate sadness and loss with freedom, appreciation and readiness to go on (like Freud's normal mourning). Neurotic organization, with excessive superego pressure and guilt: intense sadness, idealization of the therapist, feeling unworthy of what was received, clinging, a mild form of Klein's pathological mourning. BPO: severe separation anxiety, fear of abandonment, rage that destroys the good image. Narcissistic: immediate protective devaluation, with no apparent reaction.
w: Panic, rage and destroying the good image describe borderline organization.
No reaction with devaluation describes narcissistic organization.
Moderate sadness with freedom and appreciation describes the normal reaction.
k: Neurotic termination reaction: intense sadness, idealization, feeling unworthy, clinging, a mild pathological mourning.
h: Neurotic: 'I don't deserve you, please don't go.'

q: A narcissistic patient resumes after 2 months: 'To continue what I was talking about in the last session…' This illustrates:
o: 'Locking the therapist in the closet' – denial of dependency
Healthy autonomy and secure internalization of the therapist
Depressive mourning expressed through a calm return
Paranoid anxiety hidden behind a businesslike tone
e: Narcissistic patients typically show no reaction to separations: the grandiose self and defenses against dependency produce immediate protective devaluation, feeling perfectly fine or that they never needed the therapist. It is as if the patient locks the therapist in the closet during the absence and lets him out when treatment resumes, hence 'To continue what I was talking about in the last session…' after 2 months. This devaluation can conceal an underlying paranoid transference based on projected aggression.
w: Healthy autonomy would include some feeling about the absence; this is denial of dependency.
Depressive mourning would include sadness, which is absent here.
A paranoid layer may lie underneath, but the visible phenomenon is denial of dependency.
k: Narcissistic patients 'lock the therapist in the closet' during absences, denying dependency (possibly hiding paranoia).
h: Out of sight, into the closet.

q: How do borderline patients typically experience the therapist's absence?
o: As an attack, provoking rage that destroys the good image, leaving emptiness
With mild sadness and appreciation of what was received, as in normal mourning
With relief only, as a welcome break from therapy
With no reaction, as if the therapist had never left
e: For BPO patients, even minor separations provoke severe separation anxiety. The absence is experienced unconsciously as an attack, and the departed therapist becomes the persecutory object. Reactive rage is aimed at both the external therapist and his internal image: the good image is revengefully destroyed, leaving emptiness, plus fear of the therapist's revenge. Sadness is missing because the depressive position, which lets one hold a positive image of a disappointing object, has not been reached.
w: Mild sadness and appreciation describe normal mourning, not borderline reactions.
Relief alone is not the typical borderline reaction.
No reaction to the absence describes the narcissistic pattern of 'locking the therapist in the closet'.
k: Borderline: the therapist's absence feels like an attack, and rage destroys the good image, leaving emptiness.
h: 'You left me, so you're bad, and now there's nothing left of you inside.'

q: With mixed paranoid and depressive anxieties around separation, which should be interpreted first?
o: Paranoid reactions, then depressive
Depressive reactions, then paranoid
Both at once
Neither
e: Many patients have mixed paranoid and depressive anxieties around separation; the rule is to interpret the paranoid reactions first. Interpreting depressive anxieties first drives the paranoid ones underground, and the patient is not helped. Analysing paranoid fantasies first (the therapist leaves out of indifference, greed, callousness or secret contempt) strengthens the depressive ones (the therapist is exhausted or damaged by the patient), as the object being lost becomes more valued.
w: Interpreting depressive anxieties first drives the paranoid reactions underground, and the patient isn't helped.
They are addressed in sequence, paranoid first.
Both must be explored, starting with paranoid.
k: Mixed separation anxieties: interpret paranoid reactions first; this strengthens and reveals the depressive ones.
h: Clear the suspicion before you can feel the sadness.

q: Is gradually decreasing session frequency before termination recommended?
o: No – keep the same intensity to the end and work through mourning
Yes – always taper sessions to prepare for the separation
Only for neurotic patients, who tolerate separation better
Only if the patient requests fewer sessions
e: Tapering sessions to get the patient used to separation is not desirable. The ideal is to maintain the same intensity to the end and work through separation anxiety and mourning as much as possible beforehand, knowing the patient will still mourn after termination. The more these are analysed before the end, the better the patient can work them through alone. Mourning reactions are growth experiences, repeating growing up, leaving home and going to college.
w: Tapering is what the book advises against.
The recommendation applies to all, not just neurotic patients.
A patient's request would be explored, not automatically followed.
k: Don't taper before termination: keep the same intensity and work through mourning before the end.
h: Full speed to the finish line, then let them walk on alone.

q: How much advance time should be set for termination?
o: ≥3 months for extended therapy; ideally ≥6 months for multi-year treatments
≥1 week for extended therapy; ≥1 month for multi-year treatments
A single session to announce it, then the treatment ends
No notice, since a sudden end prevents regression
e: For practical purposes the therapist prepares for termination ahead of time, is predictable, and keeps the patient informed. Any extended psychotherapy needs at least 3 months between the termination decision (ideally joint) and the end; the same applies to transferring a patient seen for a year or more. Treatments lasting several years ideally need at least 6 months. The therapist observes reactions to the decision before interpreting, and long absences are also scheduled predictably.
w: Weeks or a month are far too short for working through mourning.
A single session doesn't allow working through.
Sudden endings prevent the work on termination reactions.
k: Termination notice: at least 3 months for extended therapy (or transfer after ≥1 year); ideally ≥6 months for multi-year treatment.
h: 3 for a season, 6 for the years.

q: Before analysing it, a therapist feels he failed the patient and should have loved him more. This countertransference suggests the transference is predominantly:
o: Depressive
Paranoid
Narcissistic
Psychopathic
e: The therapist's countertransference at termination is a good indicator of the dominant transference. With predominantly depressive transference, the countertransference is depressive too: before analysing it, he feels he failed the patient, that the patient deserved better, that he is abandoning her and should have loved and understood her more. With paranoid reactions, he feels the patient is escaping, devaluing, attacking by ending. With narcissistic devaluation, he devalues the patient as hopeless.
w: Paranoid transference evokes feeling attacked or escaped from, not guilt.
Narcissistic devaluation evokes the therapist devaluing the patient.
A psychopathic transference evokes suspicion of deception.
k: Termination countertransference mirrors the transference: guilt → depressive; feeling attacked → paranoid; devaluing → narcissistic.
h: The therapist's guilt echoes the patient's depressive mood.

q: What should be done in an extended stalemate when it's unclear whether maximum benefit has been reached?
o: Seek consultation and evaluate transference and countertransference
Terminate immediately, since a stalemate means maximum benefit
Double the session frequency to break the stalemate
Add medication to move the treatment forward
e: Ideally termination comes with symptom resolution, personality change and improvements in love, social relations, work and recreation. In an extended stalemate where it's unclear whether maximum benefit has been reached, careful evaluation of transference and countertransference may answer, and stalemates are reasons for consultation rather than an immediate decision. When secondary gain hasn't been analysed and treatment replaces life, great resistance to ending appears; analysing this is central and prepares for appropriate termination.
w: A stalemate is not proof of maximum benefit; it needs evaluation.
Doubling sessions isn't the recommendation; a stalemate calls for consultation and evaluation.
Medication doesn't resolve a transference stalemate; consultation and evaluation of transference do.
k: Extended stalemate → consultation plus evaluation of transference and countertransference, not an immediate decision.
h: Stuck? Get a second pair of eyes.
